# Deployment and operational contract

## Production topology

The source of truth for deployment is the private `flightstrips/infrastructure` repository, `stacks/flightstrips.yml`, watched by Portainer. Deploy three separate `nats` services, each pinned to `nats:2.15.0`, each constrained to a different labeled Swarm host and its own local persistent volume. Give each server a unique name and clustered route configuration. Keep NATS client/route/monitoring ports on the internal overlay; only backend tasks connect. Enable JetStream file storage and [encryption at rest](https://docs.nats.io/learn/security/encryption) with a versioned Swarm secret, TLS for clients and routes, an application credential with narrowly scoped subjects/JetStream APIs, and a separate operator credential. The encrypted backup includes the matching key version and a tested rotation procedure. Do not expose NATS through Traefik.

Provision three hosts before deploying the stack; a three-replica JetStream stream on three tasks scheduled to one failure domain does not meet the failure objective. Provision disk for three copies of `FS_STATE`, position KV, snapshots and navigation blobs, plus backup headroom. Do not share or move one NATS local volume between nodes. A one-shot bootstrap service creates/validates the exact resources after NATS quorum forms on stack deployment and after disaster restore; ordinary restarts retain the resource metadata and backends verify it. Swarm has no migration-style `depends_on` gate, so backend readiness remains false until bootstrap has succeeded. Two backend replicas use the existing API Traefik service, a two-gigabyte memory limit initially, and no sticky-session requirement. Backend startup validates every stream and bucket config before `/readyz` succeeds.

The application repository's release workflow currently builds and bumps `backend-migrate`, and infrastructure CI checks that migrator tag. Remove the image build, bump, stack service, Postgres secrets/volume, and migrator validation. Retire `docker-compose.prod.yml` in FlightStrips and `.github/workflows/check-drift.yml` in the infrastructure repository when the infrastructure stack becomes the only production path. Local development Compose uses the same NATS resource bootstrap and at least two backends for integration runs. The existing OIDC, AIRAC.net, Hoppie, CDM and aircraft-config inputs remain where needed. Configure Traefik's Swarm service health check with `/readyz`, a two-second interval and one-second timeout so it stops routing new connections to an unready replica; retain Docker's `/healthz` liveness probe. [Traefik's Swarm labels support service health checks](https://doc.traefik.io/traefik/reference/routing-configuration/other-providers/swarm/).

Provision a versioned 32-byte AES-256-GCM effect encryption key as a Swarm secret. All backend replicas use the same active key version during a release. Keep retired effect keys available until the last corresponding object and retained backup expire. ALB configuration and deployment remain unchanged.

## Readiness and failure behavior

`/healthz` remains process liveness. Add `/readyz`: return 200 only when NATS is connected, JetStream quorum and required resources are usable, state projection has reached the last observed stream high-water mark, the high-water check is at most two seconds old, and owner renewal/consumer delivery are healthy. Return 503 on startup replay, resource drift, connection loss, quorum loss, or projection stall. Traefik must send new WebSockets only to ready replicas. Existing sockets on a replica that loses readiness are closed with a retryable service-unavailable code; uncommitted mutations get no success response. Plugin result outbox entries survive a socket reconnect inside the same plugin process.

After one backend task dies, clients reconnect through Traefik to the other warm replica. Former ownership expires in at most eight seconds after its last accepted renewal. A replacement claim must succeed before new effects run. A lost NATS storage node leaves two of three nodes and quorum; replace its volume/replica using the documented restore procedure, not a blank task attached to an old node identity. Losing NATS quorum makes all backends unwritable and unready. A complete cluster shutdown and restart restores file-backed JetStream, then backend projections replay before traffic resumes. `FS_PRESENCE` starts empty; no old socket counts are trusted.

The initial PostgreSQL-to-NATS cutover uses stop-first backend replacement; old and new backends never serve the same production route at once. For later NATS-only rolling releases, keep `StateEvent` schema version 1 and the frontend/EuroScope Protobuf revision 2 wire schemas stable across the overlap. Deploy a reader that understands a new internal event version before enabling its writer, or use a coordinated stop-first cutover for that schema change. A backend that sees an unknown event version becomes unready. This is an internal rolling-deploy rule, not support for old browser or plugin protocols.

## Backup, restore, and capacity

- Take a daily off-cluster JetStream backup that includes `FS_STATE`, `FS_POSITIONS`, `FS_SNAPSHOT_INDEX`, and `FS_OBJECTS`. Keep 30 daily and 12 monthly backups encrypted outside the Swarm hosts. Verify every backup manifest, resource configuration, last stream sequence, and object digest.
- Restore quarterly into an isolated three-node NATS cluster and start two backends against it. Assert the same aggregate/entity counts, command outcomes, snapshot digests, navigation manifests, and retained pending deadlines. Never restore over a running production cluster.
- Retain the full `FS_STATE` log in this version. No MaxAge, MaxMsgs, purge, or subject compaction is allowed. `FS_POSITIONS` uses history 1 and epoch-separated keys so high-frequency observations do not grow an event history. Alert at 70% disk used; block release at 85% until storage is expanded. Monitor stream and object growth to size disks before exhaustion.
- Metric names/labels: `fs_nats_puback_seconds{resource}`, `fs_projection_lag_seconds{node}`, `fs_projection_behind_messages{node}`, `fs_owner_lease_remaining_seconds{aggregate_kind}`, `fs_owner_takeovers_total`, `fs_stale_epoch_rejections_total`, `fs_effects{status,type}`, `fs_snapshot_verify_failures_total`, `fs_nats_storage_bytes{resource}`, plus NATS quorum and disk metrics. Logs include command ID, aggregate, stream sequence, owner/master epoch, node ID and connection ID; never include auth tokens or private-message bodies.

## Release procedure and acceptance

The [merge and release safety contract](release-safety.md) governs every task. Preparatory tasks 00–13 may ship only while current production behavior remains intact. Tasks 14–20 are held for the coordinated activation; tasks 22/23 test that held candidate. Task 21 produces a reviewed **unmerged** production stack PR and an equivalent isolated staging stack. Completing task 21 does not deploy production; this distinction lets tasks 22 and 23 run before task 24.

1. Complete the held backend, frontend and plugin changes on the integration branch and pass pre-merge checks. Merge them as one coordinated candidate PR only after task 20 adds the release publication gate. Freeze other application releases and production deployments while this candidate is qualified. The main merge causes Release Please to open a unified release PR but does not deploy production.
2. Build the release PR head into immutable candidate backend/frontend image digests and a hash-checked plugin DLL. Run tasks 21–23 with these exact artifacts in isolated, production-equivalent staging against `nats:2.15.0`. Record the candidate workflow run/attempt, release PR tree, digests, DLL hash and stack revision. Any candidate change or rebuild invalidates affected gates. Use [the artifact handoff](release-gates-evidence.md) and bind the qualified run/attempt explicitly before promotion; never infer qualification from the newest successful run.
3. Provision and verify the three labeled production NATS hosts, persistent volumes, Swarm secrets, internal overlay, NATS routes, and empty resource bootstrap. Perform an isolated backup/restore rehearsal. Keep the task 21 production stack PR unmerged.
4. After all gates pass, merge the unified Release Please PR with no intervening `main` change. CI checks the merged tree against the tested release PR tree and promotes the tested image digests to pinned version tags without rebuilding. A mismatch blocks publication until retested. Do not merge the automatically generated infrastructure image-bump PR on its own. Task 20 must already have removed mutable `latest` candidate tags and gated plugin DLL attachment and the frontend announcement behind a manually dispatched cutover job.
5. During a planned stop-first cutover, merge the reviewed task 21 infrastructure PR with pinned matching application image tags, replacing PostgreSQL/migrator with NATS and two backend replicas and deploying the new frontend. Confirm both backend `/readyz` endpoints, NATS quorum, no SQL connection attempts, and distinct client routing. Run the manual cutover job to attach/distribute the verified plugin DLL and send the frontend announcement. No PostgreSQL data is copied into NATS; old plugin/frontends are not accepted.
6. Exercise a live test session with clients on both backend replicas. Kill one backend and one NATS node in separate drills; verify reconnect, one master, durable state, and no duplicate private message. Run a full restart drill in staging before production, not against live production sessions.
7. If a release fails before users begin new-session work, fix forward or redeploy the prior complete application/stack revision only together with its matching storage state. Once NATS-only state has accepted production writes, do not roll back to PostgreSQL or an old protocol. Fix forward from the retained NATS data and backup.

Release gates are: all task checklists complete; zero unexpected command outcomes or duplicate external effects; one backend loss and one NATS-node loss preserve acknowledged state; complete restart restores it; backup restore passes; the existing position load gates in `docs/position-performance.md` pass for 100 reports/second and the 200 reports/second burst. Current PostgreSQL measurements do not prove the new system meets these gates.
